tagline: River country, plantation architecture and the road crossed by voting rights marchers
intro: The Black Belt Nature and Heritage Trail links loops through river-shaped country across 13 Alabama counties. The Black Warrior, Tombigbee and Alabama rivers have shaped its terrain. Alabama Byways lists it among the state byways, presenting the relationship between people and land as its central subject. The tourism department highlights parks, cultural crafts and Civil Rights Movement sites. The tourism department groups more than 50 natural and cultural sites into the trail’s tours.

The Black Belt’s name comes from the black soil used to grow cotton in the nineteenth century. At Demopolis, profits from forced labor funded Gaineswood, and enslaved people performed much of its construction. Gaineswood was completed in 1861. In 1965, the Edmund Pettus Bridge became a site of the voting rights struggle when police attacked marchers heading toward Montgomery.

From Cuba, US 80 leads east to Demopolis at the meeting of the Black Warrior and Tombigbee rivers. From Gaineswood, continue east to Selma’s Edmund Pettus Bridge, then Lowndesboro’s churches. Continue toward Tuskegee, where the tourism trail includes Tuskegee National Forest. For the onward drive, US 80 connects Tuskegee through Marvyn to Phenix City on the Chattahoochee River.

moments.title: Gaineswood
moments.text: Gaineswood’s exterior looks like stone, but its decorative stucco covers brick and imitates cut blocks. Nathan Bryan Whitfield began the house in 1843 as an open-hall log dwelling; it reached its Greek Revival form in 1861. Profits from forced labor paid for the house, and enslaved people carried out much of the building work. Alabama acquired it in 1966, and the Alabama Historical Commission began restoring it. Inside, domed ceilings with central skylights distinguish the library and dining room. No quarters for the enslaved residents were preserved, although the estate retains a cook’s house, garden pavilion and gatehouse.
moments.notice: The exterior’s stucco imitates cut stone blocks over brick.

moments.title: Edmund Pettus Bridge
moments.text: The Edmund Pettus Bridge carries US 80 Business across the Alabama River, with a steel central span above the water. It opened to traffic in 1940. The central span is 250 feet long. On March 7, 1965, voting rights activists crossed it as they began a march from Selma to Montgomery. State troopers and the sheriff’s posse attacked the marchers with beatings and tear gas. On March 21, marchers crossed again under federal protection and continued to Montgomery. The west approach stands higher than the east because Selma occupies a bluff above the river.

moments.title: Lowndesboro
moments.text: The dome on Lowndesboro’s former CME Church came from Alabama’s first state capitol at Cahawba. The church dates to 1830, before residents changed the town’s name from McGill’s Hill to Lowndesboro in 1832. Along County Road 29, church buildings mark several later decades: the Presbyterian church was erected in 1850, St. Paul’s Episcopal in 1857 and the Baptist church in 1888. The United Methodist church dates to the 1880s. Nearby houses range from early cottages to columned residences, buildings of a town settled before 1820 by planters from South Carolina.
moments.notice: The former CME Church carries the dome from the first state capitol at Cahawba.
